newsitem.title: USA: Air Force probing near collision off N.Jersey.
newsitem.headline: Air Force probing near collision off N.Jersey.

text.p: The U.S. Air Force said on Thursday it was investigating an incident Wednesday involving a chartered Boeing 727 and two unarmed F-16 fighter jets, which the charter's operator described as a near collision.

A Nations Air Boeing 727, en route from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to New York, was about 70 miles (115 km) east off Atlantic City, New Jersey on Wednesday afternoon when its anti-collision alarm went off, apparently triggered by the jets.
The fighter planes were on routine exercises in the area, military and aviation officials said.

The plane, carrying about 80 passengers, was forced to dive, climb and climb again to avoid a collision, NBC-TV reported, quoting Mark McDonald, president of the Smyrna, Georgia-based company. The plane later landed safely at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
Two flight attendants and one passenger were thrown from their seats by the manuevering, the network reported, but federal aviation officials said no injuries had been reported.

Defense Department spokesman Captain Jim Knotts said the two jets were cleared by military and civilian air controllers to conduct their training mission in the area, which was scheduled at the time for exclusive use by the military.
He said the jets approached the airliner after spotting it on their radar, but retreated again after verifying visually that it was a commercial aircraft.
"One aircraft got close enough to positively identify the aircraft, saw that it was a commercial airliner and immediately broke contact," Knotts said.
The Air Force was investigating the incident, and the Federal Aviation Administration would be invited to participate in the investigation, military and aviation officials said.
McDonald said his company was upset about the incident.
"Our instrument indicated zero-zero, which means it was extremely close, because it was so close it did not read on the instrument," McDonald told NBC.
"Either the pilots screwed up or they were playing games with our airplane, and they got caught," he said.
NBC said military commanders repeatedly radioed the jets as they approached the Nations Air plane, ordering them to "break off, break off."
The two jets were on routine training flights for the New Jersey Air National Guard, a unit used to defend the coastal air space of the United States.
